title: THE TEN WOMEN DAVID LEFT BEHIND: What Happened After Absalom Used Them?
paragraphs:
THE TEN WOMEN DAVID LEFT BEHIND: What Happened After Absalom Used Them?
They survived the rooftop. Then came a sentence in Scripture so quiet—and so devastating—that most readers pass over it without realizing what happened to them next.
There were ten of them.
We do not know their names.
We do not know their ages.
We do not know which one trembled first when Jerusalem realized Absalom was coming.
We are not told what they whispered to one another inside David’s palace while the king fled.
We are not told whether any of them begged to leave with him.
We are not told whether they understood what was about to happen.
Scripture gives us almost none of those details.
And that restraint matters.
Because we must never invent a story and then call it the Bible.
But what Scripture does tell us is disturbing enough.
David was fleeing Jerusalem from his own son.

Absalom had stolen the hearts of many Israelites. The conspiracy was strengthening. Messengers arrived with the terrifying news that the people were turning toward Absalom, and David knew Jerusalem could become a battlefield.
So David ran.
His household went with him.
Almost all of it.
Then comes one sentence.
A sentence that sounds almost administrative until you know what happens next:
“And the king went forth, and all his household after him. And the king left ten women, which were concubines, to keep the house.”
—2 Samuel 15:16, KJV
Ten women.
Left behind.
To keep the house.
And if you have ever been the person everybody expected to remain strong while somebody else escaped…
If you have ever been left holding together a home somebody else walked away from…
If someone else’s war entered your life and you paid a price for decisions you did not make…
Do not rush past these women.
Because the Bible does not.
David escaped Jerusalem.
The ten remained.
Then Absalom arrived.
And what happened next was not presented in Scripture as romance.
It was political.
It was public.
It was an act designed to communicate that Absalom had irreversibly broken with his father and was claiming royal authority.

Ahithophel advised Absalom to go in to the concubines David had left behind. The purpose stated in the text was political: all Israel would hear of the rupture between father and son, strengthening Absalom’s supporters.
Then Scripture records:
“So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the top of the house, and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.”
—2 Samuel 16:22, KJV
On the roof.
In public view.
Ten women became entangled in a rebellion between powerful men.
And there is something especially chilling about the location.
The rooftop.
Because years earlier, another rooftop had appeared in David’s story.
David had seen Bathsheba bathing.
What followed included adultery, pregnancy, deception, Uriah’s death, and finally Nathan the prophet standing before David with the judgment of God.
Nathan told him that what David had done secretly would bring consequences into the open.
God declared that calamity would arise from David’s own household and that what David had done secretly would be answered before Israel in broad daylight.
Then David said five devastating words:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
And Nathan answered with something equally astonishing:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin.”
Do not miss the tension.
David was forgiven.
David was also living through consequences.
Those are not contradictions.
Grace does not mean sin was harmless.
Forgiveness does not transform evil into good.
God’s mercy toward David does not require us to pretend that nobody else was wounded by the wreckage surrounding his sin.
That is one reason these ten forgotten women matter.
They force us to look at something uncomfortable.
Sin rarely stays inside the person committing it.
We call something “private.”
God sees where the cracks are traveling.
A father’s sin can wound a household.
A leader’s corruption can wound people without power.
A husband’s secrecy can devastate a wife.
A parent’s addiction can shape a child’s memories.
A moment of lust can become years of consequences.
One person can repent and genuinely receive forgiveness while other people are still carrying scars created in the catastrophe.
That does not make grace less glorious.
It shows us why grace was so desperately necessary.
David’s sin had been forgiven.
But David’s house was bleeding.
Amnon violated Tamar.
Absalom murdered Amnon.
Absalom rebelled against David.
David fled Jerusalem.
And now ten women stood in the middle of a conflict they had not created.
They became part of Absalom’s political declaration against his father.
And then…
Absalom died.
David returned.
The rebellion was over.
The king came home.
You might expect that to be the moment everything becomes normal again.
But then Scripture gives us one of the saddest verses in David’s story.

“And David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in ward, and fed them, but went not in unto them. So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood.”
—2 Samuel 20:3, KJV
Read those final words again.
“Living in widowhood.”
The Hebrew is haunting:
אַלְמְנוּת חַיּוּת
ʾalmenût ḥayyût

The wording conveys the extraordinary condition described in the verse: widowhood while still living, even though David himself remained alive. The text also says they were צְרֻרוֹת — ṣərurôt, “shut up,” “confined,” or kept under restraint until their deaths.
Alive.
Provided for.
Yet separated.
David fed them.
David supported them.
But he did not resume sexual relations with them.
And they remained that way until death.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us every reason David made that decision.
So we should be careful where the Bible is careful.
We should not pretend we know exactly what David thought.
We should not manufacture conversations between David and these women.
We should not turn speculation into revelation.
But we can say what the text says.
They had been left behind.
Absalom publicly went in to them.
David later placed them under confinement, continued providing for them, did not return to them sexually, and they remained in that condition until death.
Ten women.
And Scripture never gives us one of their names.
That may be the part that reaches somebody reading this right now.
Because maybe you know what it feels like to become the unnamed person in somebody else’s story.
Everybody remembers the person who betrayed you.
Nobody remembers what betrayal did to you.
Everybody talks about the divorce.
Nobody knows what happened when you shut the bedroom door.
Everybody knows the scandal.
Nobody knows the person who had to wake up the next morning and continue living.
Everybody remembers the pastor who fell, the marriage that collapsed, the family that exploded, the addiction that was exposed, the affair that became public, the friendship that shattered.
But somebody else had to survive the aftermath.
Maybe that somebody was you.
You were not the headline.
You were the collateral damage.
And sometimes the deepest pain is not merely what happened.
It is what happened afterward.
Life continued.
People moved on.
Someone apologized.
Someone rebuilt their reputation.
Someone started another relationship.
Someone found another church.
Someone posted smiling pictures again.
But you were still learning how to breathe without shaking.
Still asking why God allowed it.
Still wondering whether being wounded somehow made you less worthy of being loved.
Hear this carefully:
What somebody did to you does not become your identity before Jesus Christ.
You may have been abandoned.
That is something that happened to you.
It is not your name.
You may have been betrayed.
That is part of your history.
It is not your eternal identity.
You may have been humiliated.
You may have been used.
You may have been forgotten by people who should have protected you.
But human beings do not possess the authority to write the final sentence over a life that belongs to God.
And this is where we must move beyond David.
Because David cannot carry the weight of this story.
David himself needs a Savior.
David is not Jesus.
David sinned.
Jesus did not.
David’s kingdom fractured.
Christ’s Kingdom cannot be overthrown.
David sometimes failed people entrusted to him.
Jesus Christ never abandons His people.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus is the One through whom forgiveness comes.
David could write psalms about mercy because David desperately needed mercy.
And the Son of David came centuries later not merely to discuss mercy…
but to purchase it with His blood.
This is the Gospel.
Not that broken people eventually become impressive enough for God.
Not that your scars disappear before you can approach Him.
Not that respectable people earn a seat at His table.
The Gospel announces that sinners who could never rescue themselves can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Christ entered our ruin.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And through Him there is forgiveness, reconciliation, adoption, hope, and eternal life for those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
David said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
And there is somebody reading this who needs to stop running from that sentence.
Not because your story is identical to David’s.
Not because every tragedy in your life was caused by some particular secret sin.
Scripture does not permit us to make that cruel assumption.
Sometimes you are suffering because you sinned.
Sometimes you are suffering because somebody sinned against you.
Sometimes you are living in a fallen world where bodies break, people die, relationships fracture, injustice happens, and questions remain unanswered.
But wherever you stand, the road toward God still runs through Jesus.
Maybe you are David.
You caused damage.
You crossed boundaries.
You betrayed someone.
You knew what was right and chose what was wrong.
You have been calling it a “mistake” because the word sin feels too sharp.
But grace becomes breathtaking when excuses finally die.
Repentance does not say, “I got caught.”
Repentance says:
“Against God I have sinned. I cannot undo yesterday. I cannot save myself. Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.”
Maybe you are one of the ten.
Not literally.
But emotionally.
Someone else made the decision.
You carried the consequence.
Someone else started the war.
You lived through the aftermath.
Someone else went home.
You remained trapped inside what happened.
You have wondered whether God remembers your name because the people around you seem to have forgotten it.
The ten women are unnamed in the biblical account.
But unnamed does not mean unseen by God.
That distinction matters.
Scripture repeatedly reveals a God who sees people the powerful overlook.
And ultimately, Christianity does not rest upon the promise that every earthly injustice will be repaired before we die.
It rests upon something greater:
Christ is risen.
The Judge of all the earth is not dead.
The grave does not have the final word.
Justice is not ultimately determined by whoever has the loudest voice, the strongest army, the biggest platform, or the most convincing version of events.
Jesus Christ will make all things right.
And perhaps you are neither David nor one of the ten.
Maybe you are Absalom.
Angry.
Wounded.
Hungry to prove something.
You were hurt by your father, your mother, your church, your spouse, your friend, your past.
And somewhere along the way you decided that because somebody wounded you, you were entitled to wound others.
Absalom had grievances.
But grievance did not make rebellion righteous.
Pain can explain some of our behavior.
It cannot cleanse our sin.
Only Christ can do that.
Be careful what your wound is turning you into.
There comes a terrifying moment when the wounded person can become the person doing the wounding.
That is why Jesus does not merely offer us validation.
He offers transformation.
He calls us to repent.
To forgive.
To surrender vengeance.
To bring darkness into the light.
To die to ourselves.
To follow Him.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so much.
There is enough brokenness for everyone.
A sinful father.
A rebellious son.
A kingdom tearing itself apart.
Ten women caught inside the wreckage.
And yet beyond all of them stands another King.
Jesus.
A King who does not exploit the vulnerable to secure His throne.
A King who gave Himself for His people.
A King who did not climb upward by sacrificing others.
He humbled Himself and went toward the cross.
The rulers of this world often preserve themselves by allowing others to bleed.
Jesus saved His people by bleeding Himself.
That is the difference.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people learning better behavior.
It is the announcement that our deepest problem required a crucified and risen Savior.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Stop hiding.
Maybe you have been blaming everybody except yourself.
Stop running.
Maybe someone sinned against you and you have secretly believed their sin permanently contaminated your worth.
Bring that lie to Jesus.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending you are okay.
Then do not pretend before Christ.
He already knows.
Repentance is not humiliation before a cruel God.
It is surrender before the God who already knows the truth and still opened the way home through His Son.
And if you cannot even explain what you are feeling right now, there is no need for a polished testimony.
Let other believers see it.
Let somebody pray.
Let somebody realize they are not the only person struggling in silence.
There may come a night when old memories return and you need to read these words again:
Your worst chapter does not outrank the cross.
Your deepest wound is not stronger than Christ.
Your greatest sin is not beyond the reach of the Savior when you truly turn to Him.
And your story is not finished simply because another human being wrote a terrible chapter in it.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.

But if Gospel-centered teaching has strengthened you, one practical way to support its continued spread is to share it so another wounded person, struggling believer, seeker, lukewarm Christian, or even someone who does not yet believe can encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Supporting Gospel ministry should flow from gratitude to God, never from pressure or an attempt to purchase His favor.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow deeper in Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend whose faith is fading.
Invite the believer who has become spiritually numb.
Invite the person who thinks Jesus could never want somebody with their past.
Invite the person who has never believed.
Because somewhere tonight there is another person who feels like one of those ten women.
Left behind.
Caught inside consequences they did not choose.
Living after something they thought would destroy them.
And somewhere there is another David discovering that forgiveness does not mean sin was harmless.
Somewhere there is another Absalom allowing an old wound to become tomorrow’s weapon.
And somewhere there is a person staring at a screen right now realizing:
This story is no longer about David.
It is about me.
It is about the things I have done.
The things done to me.
The things I cannot undo.
The people I cannot bring back.
The years I cannot recover.
The scars I cannot erase.
And the Savior I desperately need.
The Bible does not tell us the names of David’s ten concubines.
But it tells us the name above every name.
Jesus.
And when human beings reduce you to your scandal, your wound, your failure, your usefulness, your past, or the worst thing that ever happened to you, remember this:
The hands that were pierced for sinners are still capable of holding a story everybody else thought was finished.
